prompt: `diff` compared `SumInts` with `SumFloats` line by line. What did it find different?
hint: It printed two lines from each side.

choices.text: The loop, because a float needs another form of `range`
choices.why: `range` works the same over any slice; the loop lines were identical and `diff` did not print them.

choices.text: Only the types, in the signature and in `var total`
choices.why: Right. Two lines differ, and in both of them the only change is `int` against `float64`.

choices.text: The `return`, which converts the result to the right type
choices.why: `return total` is the same text in both; `total` already has the result's type.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: `diff` printed `1,2c1,2` and the two pairs of lines; identical text would print nothing.

prompt: `SumAny([]any{3, stock})`, with `stock` an `int64`, is wrong. Who found the mistake?
hint: `go vet && go run .` was the command.

choices.text: The compiler, which refused to build `[]any{3, stock}`
choices.why: That literal is a valid `[]any`; any value goes into one, so the program was built.

choices.text: `go vet`, which reported the `int64`
choices.why: `go vet` printed nothing and exited 0, which is why `go run` went ahead.

choices.text: The program itself, by the `default` case's panic
choices.why: Right: `panic: SumAny: cannot add int64`, at run time, on the call that happened to pass the wrong type.

choices.text: Nobody: the `int64` was converted to `float64` and added
choices.why: Nothing converts it; the type switch had cases for `int` and `float64` only, and the `default` panicked.

prompt: `ages` is a `[]int`. Why does the compiler refuse `SumAny(ages)` when `SumAny` takes `[]any`?
hint: The same refusal happened to `fmt.Println` in lesson 21.

choices.text: A `[]int` is not a `[]any`, and Go never converts one slice type into another
choices.why: Right. Each `int` could become an `any`, but the slice as a whole is a different type, so the caller copies.

choices.text: `SumAny` only accepts `float64` values
choices.why: Its type switch has an `int` case, and `SumAny(boxed)` added three `int`s to get 71.

choices.text: The call needs `ages...` to spread the slice
choices.why: `...` is for variadic parameters; `SumAny` has an ordinary slice parameter, and the types would still differ.

choices.text: The type switch has no case for `[]int`
choices.why: The switch runs at run time, on each element; the refusal came from the compiler, before anything ran.

prompt: Compared with writing `SumInts` and `SumFloats`, what does the `SumAny` version cost? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Think of the panic, the `%T` line and the `boxed` loop.

choices.text: A wrong type is found only when the program runs
choices.why: Yes: the `int64` reached the `default` case and panicked.

choices.text: The result is a `float64` whatever went in
choices.why: Yes: three `int`s gave `71 float64`.

choices.text: A caller with a `[]int` must copy it into a `[]any` first
choices.why: Yes: that is the `boxed` loop, after the compiler refused `SumAny(ages)`.

choices.text: It has to be written again for each new type
choices.why: That is the cost of the copies. `SumAny` is written once; a new type means a new `case`, not a new function.

prompt: Match each function of the standard library to the way it handles several types.
hint: `go doc` showed every one of these signatures.

pairs.right: one copy written for each element type

prompt: Why can no ordinary interface say "a type you can add with `+`"?
hint: What does an ordinary interface list?

choices.text: Interfaces cannot hold numbers, only structs
choices.why: An `any` held `3` and `1.5` in `SumAny`; an interface can hold a value of any type.

choices.text: It can: `int` and `float64` already have an `Add` method
choices.why: They have no methods at all, and lesson 25 showed you cannot add one to a type from outside your package.

choices.text: It lists methods, and `+` is an operator
choices.why: Right. That is the gap `sort.Sort` works around with `Less`, and what a type parameter's list of types fills.

choices.text: Go forbids interface parameters on functions that do arithmetic
choices.why: No such rule exists; `SumAny` took `any` values and did arithmetic after a type switch.

prompt: What is a type parameter, such as the `T` in `func Sum[T int | float64](xs []T) T`?
hint: The section starts by naming the wrong guess.

choices.text: Another way of writing `any`: it takes a value of every type
choices.why: That is the usual first guess and the reverse of the truth: `Sum` refused `int64` and `string` at compile time.

choices.text: A type decided at run time from the value passed
choices.why: Nothing is decided at run time; the compiler works `T` out from the argument when it builds the call.

choices.text: A name for a type the caller picks, checked at every call
choices.why: Right. The list after it says which types it may be, and each call is checked against that list.

choices.text: A conversion, written in brackets
choices.why: Conversions are `T(x)`, lesson 10; the brackets declare a parameter, and no value is converted.

prompt: `ints := Sum([]int{3, 4, 5})`. What did `%T` print for `ints`?
hint: The result is declared as `T`.

choices.text: `float64`
choices.why: That was `SumAny`, which had to pick one result type for every input.

choices.text: `int`
choices.why: Right: `12 int`. `T` was `int` for that call, and the result is a `T`.
`T` exists only in the source; at the call it stands for a real type, and that is what `%T` prints.

choices.text: `interface {}`
choices.why: No interface is involved; the value was never boxed into an `any`.

prompt: In `func Sum[T int | float64](xs []T) T`, the list `int | float64` is the type parameter's ___.
hint: Lesson 31 is about writing them.

prompt: What happens to `Sum([]int64{3, stock})` with `Sum` declared as `[T int | float64]`?
hint: The same `int64` made `SumAny` panic.

choices.text: It runs and returns a `float64`
choices.why: The result is a `T`, and no `T` was found: the call never compiled.

choices.text: Refused: `int64 does not satisfy int | float64`
choices.why: Right. The compiler checks each call against the list, so the mistake never reaches a running program.

choices.text: It panics at run time, like `SumAny` did
choices.why: That is the failure type parameters remove; this one is found before the program exists.

choices.text: It converts each `int64` to `int` and adds them
choices.why: Go converts nothing implicitly, lesson 10; an `int64` is simply not in the list.

prompt: A colleague widens the list to `[T int | float64 | string]`. What does `Sum([]string{"a", "b"})` do now?
hint: What does `+` do to two strings?

choices.text: Refused: `+` is not defined on strings
choices.why: `+` joins strings, so every type in the new list has one and the body still compiles.

choices.text: Compiles, and returns `"ab"`
choices.why: Right. `total` starts as `""` and `+=` joins; whether that is a sum is exactly what the list decides.

choices.text: Compiles, then panics when it reaches the strings
choices.why: Nothing is checked at run time in `Sum`; a call that compiles has already been checked.

choices.text: Returns `0`, because `var total T` starts at zero
choices.why: The zero value of a `string` is `""`, not `0`, and the loop then adds to it.

prompt: How many type parameters does `func Sort[S ~[]E, E cmp.Ordered](x S)` declare?
hint: Count the names in the square brackets, not the parameters in the round ones.

prompt: Why was `ShowAll(room, wait)` refused, when `ShowEach(room, wait)` compiled?
hint: Read the message: `does not match inferred type Celsius for T`.

choices.text: `time.Duration` has no `String` method
choices.why: It has one: `ShowEach` printed `1m30s` with it.

choices.text: `T` is one type per call, and the first argument made it `Celsius`
choices.why: Right. `wait` is a `time.Duration`, a different type, so it cannot also be the `T` of that call.

choices.text: A variadic parameter may not have a type parameter as its element type, so every such call is refused
choices.why: `ShowAll(room, room+1)` compiled and ran with exactly that signature.

choices.text: `fmt.Stringer` cannot be used as a constraint
choices.why: It can; any interface can be a constraint, and `ShowAll` compiled once its call had one type.

prompt: Which order of work does the section recommend?
hint: What was the evidence in section 02?

choices.text: Make every function generic from the start, since a type parameter costs nothing and may help one day
choices.why: It costs readability on every line, and a parameter that only ever stands for one type buys nothing back.

choices.text: Take `any` first, and switch to generics once it panics
choices.why: That waits for a run-time failure to make a decision the compiler could have made.

choices.text: Write it for one type; go generic when a second copy differs only in types
choices.why: Right. The duplication is the evidence, as the `diff` of `SumInts` and `SumFloats` was.

choices.text: Leave generics to the standard library and never write one
choices.why: The section says when to write one: containers and algorithms that would otherwise be copied per type.

prompt: Which of these are good candidates for a type parameter? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Does the code care what the type is, or only what it can do?

choices.text: A function that returns the last element of any slice
choices.why: Yes: an algorithm whose logic is the same for every element type, with `T` linking the slice to the result.

choices.text: A queue holding values of one type the caller chooses
choices.why: Yes: a container, the other case the section names.

choices.text: A function that only calls `Write` on whatever it is given
choices.why: That is behaviour: a plain `io.Writer` parameter says it and accepts more callers.

choices.text: A helper that is only ever called with a `map[string]int`
choices.why: Every caller uses one type, which is the second sign of a type parameter earning nothing.

prompt: What does the section say about `func Log[T fmt.Stringer](v T)`?
hint: How many times does `T` appear in the signature?

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: a constraint may not contain a method
choices.why: `ShowAll[T fmt.Stringer]` compiled; an interface with methods is an ordinary constraint.

choices.text: It accepts more types than `func Log(v fmt.Stringer)`
choices.why: It accepts the same ones, one type per call, which is fewer when there are several values.

choices.text: It checks the type at run time, like `SumAny`
choices.why: Constraints are checked at compile time; the run-time check comes back only with a type switch in the body.

choices.text: `T` appears once, so it does the job of `func Log(v fmt.Stringer)`
choices.why: Right. A type parameter used once links nothing to anything, and the plain interface reads more easily.

prompt: `names` is a `[]string`. What happens to `sort.Slice(&names, less)`?
hint: What type is the first parameter of `sort.Slice`?

choices.text: The compiler refuses it, because a `*[]string` is a pointer to a slice and not a slice
choices.why: The parameter is `any`, and a pointer is as good an `any` as 42 was; the compiler has nothing to refuse.

choices.text: It sorts `names` through the pointer
choices.why: `sort.Slice` wants the slice itself; its documentation says it panics if `x` is not a slice.

choices.text: It compiles, passes `go vet`, and panics when it runs
choices.why: Right. It is the 42 of section 02 in a form somebody would really write, and only running it finds out.

choices.text: `go vet` reports the pointer before it runs
choices.why: `go vet` passed `sort.Slice(42, ...)` in section 02, and it passes a pointer the same way.

prompt: `slices.Sort` sorts a slice of any element type that satisfies `cmp.___`, the constraint for types that `<` works on.
hint: It is the last word of the signature's brackets.

prompt: Why are `sort.Ints` and `sort.Float64s` still in the standard library?
hint: Read the note in `go doc sort.Ints`, and remember lesson 2.

choices.text: Code that calls them must keep compiling
choices.why: Right. The Go 1 promise keeps them, and their bodies now simply call `slices.Sort`.

choices.text: They run faster than `slices.Sort` on their own types
choices.why: They cannot: the note says each one simply calls `slices.Sort`.

choices.text: `slices.Sort` cannot sort a slice of a basic type like `int`
choices.why: `~/generics-std` sorted `[]int{41, 7, 23}` with it.

choices.text: Only they put NaN values first when sorting floats
choices.why: `go doc slices.Sort` says the same about NaNs, and `Float64s` calls it.
